Port Louis, Mauritius.

Mathieu was waiting eagerly at the table. He had never experienced Christmas before, but he was enjoying himself so far. He and the rest of his family were Hindu, but Mrs Darvi was originally from England and celebrated Christmas every year. Mathieu could smell something delightful coming from the kitchen. Mrs Darvi came into the living room carrying a large turkey. The pair of them sat down and began to eat Christmas dinner. 'I'm glad you're here Mathieu'. Mrs Darvi had been lonely for a long time. First the disappearance of her son and then the death of her husband to cancer three years ago had left her to live alone. She had spent every Christmas since in her own. Her only remaining family was back in England, and none of her husbands family lived on the mainland. The only company she had nowadays was the occasional visit from Anna. But with the arrival of Mathieu her life finally had purpose again.

Stuttgart, Germany

Anna stared at her plate. Her appetite had gone with the day she had just had. Next to her Hans tucked in greedily, not giving a care about the events earlier in the day. At least the rest of Hans' family were enjoying it. Her first year of marriage had brought nothing but strife. Her and Hans argued constantly, and the Christmas period had only heightened that. Hans had completely refused to let her go back to the Netherlands to see her family over the festive period. Anna hadn't seen her family in months, stuck in Stuttgart alone and feeling homesick. She had then had to cook Christmas dinner without a single word of thanks from Hans. Her thoughts turned to the wonderful Christmas she had in Mauritius, with Charles and his family. She missed him so much. She wished she was back in Mauritius, spending Christmas with Charles. Her eyes began to water, as she stood up, took off her wedding ring and walked out the door.

Unknown, Unknown

A shaft of light filled his vision. The small hatch at the bottom of the door had opened. The light blinded him until his eyes grew accustomed to his surroundings. A small bowl of cold rice was shoved into the room through the slot. He picked up the bowl, devouring the contents hungrily. He couldn't remember how long ago this routine had begun. He left the empty bowl by the door, as he went back to his pathetic excuse of a mattress. The springs always dug into his back, he barely slept. He laid down, trying to get some sleep. He knew he wouldn't. He hated this cell. It was cold, damp and uncomfortable. He almost wished he had died in that storm.
